name: Shinshu Juwari Soba Ten, Nagano Station Branch (信州十割そば てん 長野駅前店)

claims.text: 打ち粉不使用 (no dusting flour) and the shop serves only 100% buckwheat jūwari soba — no wheat noodles on the menu — so shared-boiling-water contamination from wheat soba is largely eliminated.
Dedicated vs shared boiling water is not explicitly stated; still worth asking staff to boil in a clean pot / fresh water for a celiac guest.

Tsuyu (もりつゆ / くるみつゆ / とろろ) at the Nagano branch is not confirmed to be tamari/gluten-free; standard soba tsuyu uses wheat soy sauce. Only the separate Karuizawa branch publicly states 「天ぷら、そばつゆも完全グルテンフリー」.
Standard soba tsuyu likely contains bonito (katsuo) dashi; no vegan-dashi option documented.
No documented formal allergen protocol; ordering is via tablet. GF is a promoted feature (soba + tempura) but tsuyu handling for celiac must be confirmed with staff on-site.
「長野県・木島平産そば粉100％で作る十割そば」— only 100% buckwheat jūwari soba served, with 打ち粉不使用 (no dusting flour).
「天ぷらもそば粉と米粉が衣に使用され、グルテンフリー」— tempura batter is buckwheat + rice flour, fried in rice oil (米油).

The soba noodles are 二八 (80% buckwheat, 20% wheat); wheat flour is used in-house for noodle production, so the entire kitchen environment involves wheat. No cross-contamination controls have been documented by any source.
Standard Japanese soy sauce (wheat-containing shoyu) is used in the tsuyu dipping broth; no tamari or GF soy sauce alternative is mentioned anywhere.
Bonito dashi (厚削りの本枯れ節) is the foundation of all broth preparations; there is no plant-based broth option, and fish-based dashi permeates even light menu items.
One tourism listing notes the restaurant 'welcomes consultation on religious dietary requirements,' but no specific allergy protocol or trained allergy-handling procedure is documented.
Soba is made fresh daily and sold out when it runs out — no pre-made, stored product.

name: すや亀 食味処 (Suyakame Shokumidokoro)

claims.text: Miso udon is a core menu item served in the same small kitchen (approximately 17 seats). Wheat contamination risk from shared prep surfaces and cookware is unverified and undocumented.

No tamari or gluten-free soy sauce is mentioned anywhere on the official site or in any reviews. Standard Japanese soy sauce (醤油, containing wheat) is the expected seasoning for grilled rice balls, dengaku glaze, and marinades.
Menu includes miso-marinated fish (銀だら定食, silver cod), miso-braised pork, and egg dishes alongside any plant-forward options; shared cookware contact is undisclosed.
No allergen menu, allergy handling policy, or staff allergy training is mentioned on the official website, Tabelog, or any review source found.

The core product — Shinshu miso — is traditionally made from soybeans, rice, and salt with no wheat in the paste itself, which is a positive baseline if wheat-free soy sauce were used. However, this has not been confirmed for the kitchen's cooking.

name: 手揉み中華そば まるもも 長野店 (Temomi Chuka Soba Marumomo Nagano)

claims.text: Hand-kneaded wheat noodles are the restaurant's defining product — wheat flour is present throughout the kitchen. No separation of prep areas noted.
No soy sauce type disclosed, but standard Chinese-style ramen tare almost certainly uses wheat-containing soy sauce. No tamari or gluten-free soy sauce mentioned anywhere.
All broths are pork- and chicken-based; there is no plant-based broth option. Lard (背脂) variants mentioned. Vegan diners have no safe option here.
The official site notes customers with dietary restrictions should contact the restaurant directly (要問合せ), but no structured allergen protocol or allergy-trained staff information is documented.

name: タイレストラン トムヤムクン (Thai Restaurant Tom Yam Kun)

claims.text: No dedicated gluten-free kitchen or allergen separation confirmed. Small kitchen environment with no published allergen protocol.

Thai cooking traditionally uses fish sauce (nam pla) rather than wheat-based soy sauce for seasoning, reducing the main wheat vector compared to Japanese cuisine. However, some Thai curry pastes and Japanese-market condiments used in Thai restaurants can contain wheat — not verified for this kitchen.
Fish sauce is used across all savory dishes. No plant-based cooking separation noted.
No allergy handling policy found. Staff communication is likely Japanese-only; detailed allergy dialogue may be challenging.

Fish-sauce-based seasoning (rather than wheat soy sauce) is structurally more GF-friendly than most Japanese restaurant kitchens, giving a reasonable baseline for wheat avoidance on dishes verified dish-by-dish.

name: ザ フジヤ ゴホンジン（藤屋御本陳） (The Fujiya Gohonjin)

claims.text: Pasta — made with wheat flour — is the central product of this Italian kitchen. Cross-contamination with gluten must be assumed to be high. The restaurant's own FAQ confirms it cannot accommodate gluten-free diets at lunch and offers no course-menu modifications for GF at dinner.
Italian cuisine style; soy sauce is not a primary concern here, but wheat-containing pasta, bread/focaccia, and flour-based sauces are used throughout the kitchen.
No vegan or vegetarian menu exists. Meat, seafood, dairy, and eggs are core to most dishes. Vegetarian accommodation is explicitly declined at lunch.

Guests with food allergies are asked to inform staff (食材アレルギーをお持ちの方はスタッフにお申しつけください). Allergy accommodations and religious dietary needs can be discussed, but require a phone reservation rather than online booking.
Staff can provide ingredient details during your visit, but the FAQ makes clear that structural GF or vegetarian accommodation is very limited.
English menus and English-speaking staff are available, making allergy communication somewhat easier for non-Japanese speakers.
For dinner, some a la carte items may be naturally suitable depending on selection; direct phone contact before visiting is the recommended path for any dietary need.

Wheat flour is the core ingredient of every item on the menu — pizza dough, bread rolls, and sandwich bread are all made with domestic wheat. No gluten-free alternatives exist. Cross-contamination throughout the entire kitchen is certain.
No soy sauce reported in this Italian/pizza format, but wheat is omnipresent in the bread and dough base. Wheat avoidance is not possible here.
Cheese is standard on pizzas and in many sandwiches; prosciutto, bacon, and salami are common sandwich fillings. Dairy cross-contact is unavoidable in this kitchen.
No allergy menu, allergy card, or staff allergy-handling protocol has been reported in any source. Communication is entirely in Japanese; allergy requests should be made by phone in advance.

Ingredients are carefully sourced: organically grown or pesticide-free vegetables, artisan cheeses from small producers in Okayama, Hokkaido, and Nagano, and dough made from domestic wheat with natural yeast and natural sea salt — a clean, additive-free kitchen.

name: 戸隠つきや 門前店 (Togakure Tsukiya Monzen)

claims.text: No information found about separate prep surfaces or fryers for gluten-free orders. Tempura (wheat batter) is cooked in the kitchen alongside soba, raising cross-contamination concern.
Tsuyu dipping broth for soba almost certainly contains standard Japanese soy sauce (shoyu), which is brewed with wheat. No tamari or GF soy sauce alternative has been documented at this restaurant.
Fish-based dashi (katsuobushi) is the standard base for soba tsuyu in Japan and is very likely present in the broth here. No vegan dashi alternative is mentioned in any source.

No allergy handling protocol, allergen menu, or staff training information has been documented in any available source. Contact the restaurant directly at 026-233-8028 before visiting if dietary restrictions are serious.
Buckwheat (soba) itself is naturally gluten-free, and plain cold zaru soba without dipping broth could be lower risk — though cross-contamination from shared kitchen equipment remains unconfirmed.
